title: Growing One Cell into a Colony
endLine: Growing one cell into a colony tests potential, not fate.

scenes.tts: Can one cell produce several cell types? In a crowded dish, neurons and pigment cells sit side by side. You cannot tell if one ancestor made both, or separate specialists grew together.
scenes.caption: Can one cell produce several cell types? In a crowded dish, neurons and pigment cells sit side by side. You cannot tell if one ancestor made both, or separate specialists grew together.
scenes.visual: Top-down schematic view of one round culture dish filling 65% of the frame height, containing gently drifting schematic neurons (branched blue cells) and pigment cells (dark rounded cells) mixed together. In the first 5 seconds, a bright ring isolates one cell with a question mark ('One ancestor?'). The highlight then splits smoothly into two schematic branching paths beside the dish: one cell branching into both types versus two separate specialists.
scenes.narration: Can one cell produce several cell types? In a crowded dish, neurons and pigment cells sit side by side. You cannot tell if one ancestor made both, or separate specialists grew together.

scenes.visual: The carried culture dish stays centred and dims softly behind high-contrast title text 'Growing One Cell into a Colony'; one glowing cell stays pulsing gently at the centre of the dish.

scenes.tts: To find out, plate cells sparsely so each sits alone. Over days, one cell divides into a clone, a colony from one cell. One division proves little, because short-lived progenitors also divide briefly before differentiating. Repeated growth and replating tests whether a stem-cell pool persists.
scenes.caption: To find out, plate cells sparsely so each sits alone. Over days, one cell divides into a clone, a colony from one cell. One division proves little, because short-lived progenitors also divide briefly before differentiating. Repeated growth and replating tests whether a stem-cell pool persists.
scenes.visual: The crowded dish clears and dilutes until single schematic cells sit well apart on the dish floor (label: 'Single cell'). One cell brightens and divides repeatedly over a schematic day counter into a tight cluster of descendants (label: 'Clone'). On 'short-lived progenitors', a second schematic cell divides briefly, differentiates and stops. On 'Repeated growth and replating', one cell lifts out of the first clone into a fresh carried dish and grows a second clone (label: 'Self-renewal test').
scenes.narration: To find out, plate cells sparsely so each sits alone. Over days, one cell divides into a clone, a colony from one cell. One division proves little, because short-lived progenitors also divide briefly before differentiating. Repeated growth and replating tests whether a stem-cell pool persists.

scenes.tts: Changing the dish tests other growth habits. A normal fibroblast, a connective-tissue cell, divides only when anchored. In soft agar, a gel with no anchor, normal fibroblasts stop. A transformed cell, with tumour-like habits, needs no anchor and forms a colony.
scenes.caption: Changing the dish tests other growth habits. A normal fibroblast, a connective-tissue cell, divides only when anchored. In soft agar, a gel with no anchor, normal fibroblasts stop. A transformed cell, with tumour-like habits, needs no anchor and forms a colony.
scenes.visual: The carried round dish smoothly tilts into a side cross-section filling 65% of the frame height. First, a flat schematic fibroblast anchors to the dish floor and divides into two (label: 'Anchored'). Then translucent blue gel fills the dish (label: 'Soft agar, schematic'): the normal fibroblast floats unanchored and stays single, while a bright orange transformed cell suspended in the same gel divides into a round floating colony (label: 'Transformed colony').
scenes.narration: Changing the dish tests other growth habits. A normal fibroblast, a connective-tissue cell, divides only when anchored. In soft agar, a gel with no anchor, normal fibroblasts stop. A transformed cell, with tumour-like habits, needs no anchor and forms a colony.

scenes.tts: Now take one neural crest cell, a migrating embryonic cell, alone in a dish. It grows a colony of both neurons and pigment cells. Does that show this cell would have made both in the embryo?
scenes.caption: Now take one neural crest cell, a migrating embryonic cell, alone in a dish. It grows a colony of both neurons and pigment cells. Does that show this cell would have made both in the embryo?
scenes.visual: The dish rotates smoothly back to top-down view with one bright schematic neural crest cell alone at the centre. As the narrator describes its growth, the cell divides into one mixed schematic colony containing both branched blue neurons and dark pigment cells. Above the dish, high-contrast text fades in: 'Would it make both in the embryo?'
scenes.narration: Now take one neural crest cell, a migrating embryonic cell, alone in a dish. It grows a colony of both neurons and pigment cells. Does that show this cell would have made both in the embryo?

scenes.visual: The carried dish with the single mixed neuron-and-pigment colony stays on screen with slow ambient cell drift (schematic), while the question 'Would it make both in the embryo?' remains visible and a thin circular progress arc fills smoothly over 4.5 seconds.

scenes.tts: Not necessarily. Growing one cell into a colony tests potential, not fate. Culture shows what a cell can make under one condition. In the embryo, route and surroundings might choose only one type. To learn what it did make, label it in place and find its descendants later.
scenes.caption: Not necessarily. Growing one cell into a colony tests potential, not fate. Culture shows what a cell can make under one condition. In the embryo, route and surroundings might choose only one type. To learn what it did make, label it in place and find its descendants later.
scenes.visual: The dish shifts left (label: 'Potential: dish') and a schematic embryo outline appears on the right (label: 'Fate: embryo'). Inside the dish, the mixed colony glows with both cell types; inside the schematic embryo, a single cell travels along one highlighted route and turns into only one cell type as surroundings cue it. On 'label it in place', a bright marker tag attaches to the cell inside the embryo and stays on its descendants as it divides.
scenes.narration: Not necessarily. Growing one cell into a colony tests potential, not fate. Culture shows what a cell can make under one condition. In the embryo, route and surroundings might choose only one type. To learn what it did make, label it in place and find its descendants later.

scenes.tts: Two traps can mislead. Proportions in a mixed culture can shift through faster division or death, without any fate change. Follow clones instead, counting every cell at start and end. Dish conditions can also trigger fates hard to find in living animals. Helper cells boosting colonies show they can help, not that living tissue requires them.
scenes.caption: Two traps can mislead. Proportions in a mixed culture can shift through faster division or death, without any fate change. Follow clones instead, counting every cell at start and end. Dish conditions can also trigger fates hard to find in living animals. Helper cells boosting colonies show they can help, not that living tissue requires them.
scenes.visual: Back in the carried dish, split cleanly into two sequential schematic checks. First, a crowded mixed dish (label: 'Mixed proportions') blurs into ambiguity, as some cells divide faster and others die off, then morphs into a sparse dish with start-and-end counts for each clone (label: 'Count every cell'). Second, the dish fills with tinted fluid and a schematic cell morphs into an unusual star-shaped dish-only type that fades beside an embryo outline (label: 'Dish-only fate'); helper cells then appear beside a growing colony with a label 'Sufficiency, not requirement'.
scenes.narration: Two traps can mislead. Proportions in a mixed culture can shift through faster division or death, without any fate change. Follow clones instead, counting every cell at start and end. Dish conditions can also trigger fates hard to find in living animals. Helper cells boosting colonies show they can help, not that living tissue requires them.

scenes.tts: With those guards, colony assays unlocked findings. In nineteen eighty-eight, Anne Baroffio, Elisabeth Dupin and Le Douarin plated single quail crest cells. They analysed two hundred forty-three clones. Some made one neuron type; others made several neuron types, non-neuronal cells and pigment-making melanocytes.
scenes.caption: With those guards, colony assays unlocked findings. In 1988, Anne Baroffio, Elisabeth Dupin and Le Douarin plated single quail crest cells. They analysed 243 clones. Some made one neuron type; others made several neuron types, non-neuronal cells and pigment-making melanocytes.
scenes.visual: The carried dish shows a faint schematic feeder layer of flat 3T3 cells and single quail crest cells plated across it (source tag: 'Baroffio, Dupin & Le Douarin, 1988'). A schematic 7-to-10-day bar fills as colonies expand, and a counter climbs to 243 clones. Three highlighted schematic clones enlarge in place: one with a single neuron type, one mixed with several neuron types, grey non-neuronal cells and dark melanocytes, and an intermediate clone between them.
scenes.narration: With those guards, colony assays unlocked findings. In 1988, Anne Baroffio, Elisabeth Dupin and Le Douarin plated single quail crest cells. They analysed 243 clones. Some made one neuron type; others made several neuron types, non-neuronal cells and pigment-making melanocytes.

scenes.tts: Soft agar surprised, too. A transforming growth factor, or T G F, was thought to come from cancer cells. In nineteen eighty-one, Anita Roberts and Michael Sporn found such activity in healthy mouse organs.
scenes.caption: Soft agar surprised, too. A transforming growth factor, or TGF, was thought to come from cancer cells. In 1981, Anita Roberts and Michael Sporn found such activity in healthy mouse organs.
scenes.visual: The carried dish tilts back to its soft-agar side cross-section (source tag: 'Roberts & Sporn, 1981 & 1983'). A small tag 'thought: cancer-cell product' sits over the dish, then drops of extract from a schematic healthy mouse organ (tag '1981') enter the gel and a suspended fibroblast begins to grow into a colony (schematic).
scenes.narration: Soft agar surprised, too. A transforming growth factor, or TGF, was thought to come from cancer cells. In 1981, Anita Roberts and Michael Sporn found such activity in healthy mouse organs.

scenes.tts: In nineteen eighty-three, they showed the original activity was two proteins, T G F alpha and beta. T G F beta raised large colonies only alongside T G F alpha or epidermal growth factor.
scenes.caption: In 1983, they showed the original activity was two proteins, TGF-α and TGF-β. TGF-β raised large colonies only alongside TGF-α or epidermal growth factor.
scenes.visual: Same soft-agar cross-section. The activity splits (tag '1983') into two colour-coded schematic droplets labelled 'TGF-α' and 'TGF-β' (no molecular structures). With 'TGF-β' alone, the suspended fibroblast stays single; when 'TGF-α' or 'EGF' joins it, the cell grows into a large suspended soft-agar colony.
scenes.narration: In 1983, they showed the original activity was two proteins, TGF-α and TGF-β. TGF-β raised large colonies only alongside TGF-α or epidermal growth factor.

scenes.tts: Colonies also guided reprogramming. In two thousand six, Kazutoshi Takahashi and Shinya Yamanaka delivered twenty-four stem-cell genes into mouse fibroblasts. They linked a stem-cell gene to drug resistance, so only cells activating it formed colonies. Leaving out one factor at a time left four that made induced pluripotent stem cells.
scenes.caption: Colonies also guided reprogramming. In 2006, Kazutoshi Takahashi and Shinya Yamanaka delivered 24 stem-cell genes into mouse fibroblasts. They linked a stem-cell gene to drug resistance, so only cells activating it formed colonies. Leaving out one factor at a time left four that made induced pluripotent stem cells.
scenes.visual: The carried dish returns to top-down view containing schematic elongated mouse fibroblasts (source tag: 'Takahashi & Yamanaka, 2006'). A schematic badge '24 genes' enters the cells, followed by a pale drug wash across the dish: cells not activating the linked gene fade away, while surviving cells grow into bright round colonies. The badge counts down one by one until '4 factors' remain glowing over thriving schematic iPS cell colonies.
scenes.narration: Colonies also guided reprogramming. In 2006, Kazutoshi Takahashi and Shinya Yamanaka delivered 24 stem-cell genes into mouse fibroblasts. They linked a stem-cell gene to drug resistance, so only cells activating it formed colonies. Leaving out one factor at a time left four that made induced pluripotent stem cells.

scenes.tts: Every colony reveals what one isolated cell can do. To learn what that cell did, look back inside the living body.
scenes.caption: Every colony reveals what one isolated cell can do. To learn what that cell did, look back inside the living body.
scenes.visual: The carried culture dish returns to centre screen with one cell branching smoothly into a glowing schematic colony (label: 'Potential'), paired gently beside the schematic embryo outline (label: 'Living tissue'). Both stay in slow ambient motion as the frame dims smoothly toward the end card.
scenes.narration: Every colony reveals what one isolated cell can do. To learn what that cell did, look back inside the living body.

scenes.visual: Clean dark end card with a subtle, slowly drifting schematic outline of one cell branching into a colony behind full-contrast centred text reading verbatim: 'Growing one cell into a colony tests potential, not fate.'
